sentences.text: Alnashetri was a tiny, non-avian coelurosaur dinosaur that stood just 35 centimeters tall and measured only 60 centimeters in length.
This makes it the smallest alvarezsauroid known to science.
Its name means slender thighs, a reference to its long, thin hind legs.
The species name honors the village of Cerro Policía, which assisted researchers during fieldwork.
Scientists Peter J. Makovicky, Sebastián Apesteguía, and Federico A. Gianechini first named this extinct alvarezsauroid theropod in 2012.
The genus contains a single species, Alnashetri cerropoliciensis, known from two specimens, one of which features articulated hind limbs.
A more complete skeleton was unearthed in 2014 and formally described in 2026.
Fossils were recovered from red sandstones in the upper section of the Candeleros Formation near the boundary with the Huincul Formation.
The holotype specimen includes a partial left femur, distal parts of both tibiae, a right fibula, proximal tarsals, a nearly complete right metatarsus, and parts of the left foot bones.
A more complete specimen, MPCA Pv377, was inferred to be a female.
Phylogenetic analysis initially placed Alnashetri within the group Alvarezsauroidea.
Later studies recovered Alnashetri as a basal alvarezsauroid, more derived than Xiyunykus and Bannykus but outside the family Alvarezsauridae.
The parent group of the genus Alnashetri is Alvarezsauridae.
Alnashetri is classified as a reptile.
While originally thought to be Late Cretaceous, the age of Alnashetri was re-dated to the early Albian, approximately 111.4 to 106.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether the evidence supporting Alnashetri's placement in Alvarezsauroidea is reliable, as it relies heavily on ankle anatomy which may produce false results.
Due to the fragmentary nature of the holotype skeleton, Alnashetri lacks synapomorphies that would allow for a precise assignment to a particular ceratosaurian clade.
